Odesa Tairivske Municipal Cemetery – Jewish section

Jewish Cemetery · Odesa, Ukraine

Demolished. This section was established in the 1990s; aside from one tombstone relocated from another cemetery (dated 1929), its oldest gravestone dates to 1995, its newest to 2018. Odesa's Jewish community (known as Khadzhibei under earlier Turkish rule) predates 1789, when Russian troops captured the Turkish fortress there; population reached 146 (10%) by 1795, with a synagogue, cemetery, Talmud Torah, and hospital operating by the early 19th century. From the mid-19th century, Jews dominated trade sectors including cattle and grain export, alongside medicine, law, engineering, and architecture; 44 synagogues operated by 1886, and educational infrastructure grew to 200 hederim and 40 elementary schools by the early 20th century. Population reached 138,935 (34%) by 1897, plus 1,049 Karaites. A 1905 pogrom killed 300 Jews; post-1917 revolution self-defense formations organized. Odesa became a major Zionist center from the 1889 founding of the Benei Moshe society and the 'Odessa Committee,' drawing prominent figures including Tel Aviv's first mayor Meir Dizengoff, Zalman Epstein, Chaim Nachman Bialik, and Ze'ev Jabotinsky. Early 1920s Soviet policy briefly encouraged Yiddish in official use, including court and militia correspondence and teacher-college departments; a Museum of Jewish Culture opened in 1928. Population reached 200,961 (33%) by 1939. Following Nazi-Romanian occupation from October 16, 1941, an estimated 40,000+ Jews were executed, burned in barracks, or shot between October 23-25, 1941; a Slobodka ghetto formed January 10-11, 1942, funneling residents toward execution sites, including Berezovka, where up to 33,000 Odesa Jews were murdered in early 1942. Official ghetto operations ended June 10, 1942, though the last transport departed June 23. Jews began returning after April 10, 1944; by 1958, 102,000 Jews lived in Odesa.
